title: 米国頼みの高市外交 限界浮き彫り
body:
高市早苗首相は就任後初の訪中で中国の習近平国家主席と握手を交わすにとどまり、短時間の会談も実現できなかった。関係改善への期待もあったが、中国側の空港での出迎えは各国首脳と比べて明らかに簡素で、首相周辺は「非礼だ」と憤る。米中ロ3カ国首脳会談に注目が集まる中、トランプ米大統領とも短時間の懇談をしただけで、米国頼みの高市外交の限界も浮き彫りになった。【写真】握手を交わす高市首相と中国の習近平国家主席「中国は重要な隣国。懸案と課題があるからこそ対話し、意思疎通をしていくことが重要だ」
高市氏は19日、中国・深圳でのアジア太平洋経済協力会議（APEC）首脳会議出席後の記者会見で、関係改善に意欲を示した。議長として出迎える習氏と2度握手し、その際に招待のお礼と開催への祝意を伝えたことを明らかにした。ただ習氏がそれに答えることはなかったようだ。主要国の中で習氏との個別会談がなかったのは日本のみ。空港の出迎えも各国首脳は若者たちが歓迎して花束を贈呈されたが、高市首相にはいずれもなく「冷遇」を印象づけた。中国側が出迎えたのは引退した外交官で、日本外務省関係者は「完全な格下扱いだ」と不満を漏らした。中国メディア関係者は「外交儀礼を欠いたと批判を浴びれば中国にとってマイナス。どうやって他国と差をつけるかは計算ずくだ」と解説した。
高市政権の内閣支持率は高止まりし、厳しい対中姿勢を評価する声も多い。官邸幹部は「台湾問題への姿勢を変えたわけではない。首相答弁の撤回も修正もできない」と強気だ。中国側も態度を軟化させる兆しはなく、関係の冷え込みは長期化する可能性が高い。高市首相は19日の会見で一連の外交日程で「力強い日本外交を展開できた」と手応えを語った。
ただ、歩調を合わせて中国と対峙（たいじ）するはずだったトランプ氏は習氏との関係強化に前のめりになっており、フィリピンでの東南アジア諸国連合（ASEAN）首脳会議のタイミングを狙った会談も短時間に終わった。19日に深圳でトランプ氏と習氏が米中ロ首脳会談のほかに個別に約1時間会談したのとは対照的だった。日本は「蚊帳の外」に置かれているようにも見える。大国化する中国とどう向き合うのか。米国追従だけではない外交戦略の確立が迫られている。

title: 日経平均 一時2800円以上値下がり
body: きょうの東京株式市場で日経平均株価は一時、2800円以上値下がりしました。19日のニューヨーク市場では、AI開発大手のアンソロピックが上場したことを受けて一時はダウ平均株価などが上昇したものの、その後利益を確定する売り注文が広がり、大幅安となりました。【写真で見る】月1万円投資で「450万円⇒7800万円」勝つ人・負ける人の“決定的な差”こうした流れを受けてきょうの東京市場でも、取引開始直後からほぼ全面安となり、日経平均株価は取引時間中としてアメリカの中間選挙後に値下がり続いた11月6日以来の安値をつけました。

title: 楽天証券へ訴訟準備 1.5万人登録
body: ネット証券大手の楽天証券で最大で1572万件の顧客情報が流出した可能性がある問題で、都内の弁護士が集団訴訟を準備するウェブサイトを立ち上げました。【写真で見る】SNSで話題!品薄になっている「専用ノート」楽天証券は今月17日、社内のシステムが不正アクセスを受けて、最大で1572万口座の顧客情報が流出した可能性があると明らかにしています。楽天証券によりますと、▼およそ447万口座で氏名や生年月日、住所、金融資産額、それに年収などの情報と、▼およそ1125万口座で口座番号にあたる「部店・お客様コード」とログインIDの情報が漏えいした可能性があるということです。この問題を受けて、都内の弁護士が楽天証券に対する集団訴訟を準備するウェブサイトを立ち上げました。サイトを立ち上げた牧野裕貴弁護士によりますと、きょう（20日）午前中の時点で1万5000人を超える人が登録をしているということです。牧野弁護士は、「個人情報の漏えい問題は、プライバシーの問題だけにとどまらず、治安の問題になりつつある。情報を漏えいした企業の責任を追及していかなければならない」と話しています。牧野弁護士は、カーシェア大手の「タイムズカー」で不正アクセスによって免許証の画像を含む個人情報およそ660万件が流出した問題でも、運営会社の「パーク24」などへの集団提訴を呼びかけるウェブサイトを立ち上げ、訴訟に向けた準備を進めています。

title: 人気の米のカバ死ぬ ニット帽誤飲
body: 【AFP＝時事】米オハイオ州のシンシナティ動物園は19日、ニット帽を誤ってのみ込んだカバの「フィオナ」について、獣医師らが何度も取り除こうとしたものの成功せず、死んだと発表した。【写真】麻薬王のカバ、狩猟で駆除へ コロンビア裁判所フィオナは9歳のナイルカバで、ソーシャルメディア上での愛らしい振る舞いで親しまれ、世界的な人気を集めていた。先週、ニット帽をのみ込んだ後、食欲が落ち始めた。同園はソーシャルメディアへの投稿で、「非常に悲しいことに、素晴らしい獣医師と飼育員のチームがフィオナを救おうと何度も試みたが、助からなかったという痛ましい知らせを伝えなければならない」と述べた。さらに「先週、誤って飼育エリアに入り込んだ帽子をフィオナがのみ込んだ後、獣医師らは救うためにできる限りのことをした」と説明した。「帽子を体外に排出させようと何度も試みたが、うまくいかなかった。チームはきょう、フィオナを救おうと必要な支持療法を行ったが、成功せず、回復することはなかった」フィオナの窮状を受け、世界中から応援の声が殺到した。インスタグラムでは、あるユーザーが「カバがうんちをするよう、こんなに祈ったことはない」と書き込んだ。一方、子どもの親を非難する声も上がった。動物園によると、子どもが帽子を空中に投げたところ、シーリングファンに引っ掛かり、飛ばされてしまったという。同園の動物医療責任者マイク・ウェニンガー氏によると、フィオナは24時間体制で監視と治療を受け、浣腸（かんちょう）や鎮痛薬、吐き気止めの投与などが行われていた。フィオナはすでに成獣だったため、外科手術は現実的な選択肢とはみなされなかった。また、鎮静剤を投与した上で、肛門から全長約2.7メートルの内視鏡を挿入して帽子を取り出そうとしたが、成功しなかった。フィオナは2017年1月に誕生した。シンシナティ動植物園でナイルカバが生まれたのは75年ぶりだった。早産で生まれたフィオナは当初、立ち上がることも、母親のビビから母乳を飲むこともできなかったが、その後、目覚ましい回復を遂げた。フィオナと2022年生まれの弟フリッツは、スイカを豪快に食べたり、ティラピアに囲まれて水槽の中を歩いたり、葉を食べようと体を伸ばしたりする動画で、世界中の人々を魅了してきた。【翻訳編集】 AFPBB News

title: 空港で靴磨き 航空会社の元社長
body:
北九州空港2階の出発ロビーに、早朝から無料で「靴の汚れ落とし」をする男性がいる。彼の正体は、北九州市に本社を置く航空会社「スターフライヤー」の元社長・松石禎己さん、73歳。【写真を見る】実際に靴磨きをする様子。客の中には元社長だと知らない人も顧問を退任した翌月の2021年7月に活動を始めて、これまでに磨いた靴は5000人分を超える。なぜ元社長はボランティアで靴を磨き続けるのか。そこには、社長時代から変わらない熱い思いと、一期一会の楽しみがあった。■5時半から11時半まで「靴の汚れ落とし」
外はまだ真っ暗な、朝5時半。北九州空港がオープンすると、松石さんは靴磨きの道具を手に2階の出発ロビーへ向かう。手際よく道具を並べる傍らに飾られているのは、華やかな花かごやハロウィンの雑貨、歌う鳥のオブジェ。「花かごはスタフラを退職するときに社員たちがくれたもの。季節の雑貨は客室乗務員が持って来てくれて、鳥は常連のお客さんにもらいました。ありがたいよね」とちょっと照れたように話す。看板に「靴磨き」ではなく「靴の汚れ落とし」と掲げているのには理由がある。「私は靴磨きの教育を受けたプロじゃないから。控えめでアマチュアっぽい響きがいいでしょ」と笑う。
松石さんがここで活動するのは月に4日ほど、朝5時半から11時半頃まで。2026年5月までは平日ほぼ毎日通っていたが、6月から学校法人の監査室長として週3日働くようになり、活動日が減った。1日に訪れる客は平均5、6人。出張や帰省、旅行など、さまざまな理由で空港を訪れる人たちだ。「誰も来ない日も何度かあったけど、ここにいるだけで面白いからいいんですよ」。朝6時半、この日最初のお客さんは、東京へ出張に向かう男性経営者。松石さんが空港で靴磨きをしていると知り、「ぜひ一度話してみたい」と立ち寄ったという。
作業は5〜10分ほど。松石さんは手を動かしながら、男性の話に耳を傾ける。「靴がきれいになると、朝から気持ちがいいですね。ありがとうございました」。そう言って搭乗口へ向かう男性を、松石さんは笑顔で見送った。男性が去ると、松石さんはノートを取り出し、ペンを走らせた。「すぐ忘れちゃうからね」。訪れた人の特徴や交わした会話を書き留めるノートは、すでに10冊目になった。1953年、長崎県平戸市生まれ。叔父がパイロットだったことから、幼い頃から航空業界に関心を持っていた。九州大学工学部航空工学科を卒業後、1975年に全日本空輸(ANA)に入社。整備部門などを経て、スカイネットアジア航空(現ソラシドエア)の経営再建に携わり、ANAエアロサプライシステム社長などを歴任した。

title: 露 クリミア橋攻撃受け報復宣言
body: ロシアのプーチン大統領は、ウクライナ軍によるクリミア橋への攻撃に対して、強い報復措置を取る考えを示しました。ロシアが併合したウクライナ南部クリミア半島とロシア本土をつなぐクリミア橋は、16日、17日、19日と相次いでウクライナ軍のドローンやミサイルによる攻撃を受け、自動車と鉄道の通行が停止するなどの影響が出ました。ウクライナのゼレンスキー大統領はクリミア橋を「ロシア軍の主要な輸送路」とし、今回の攻撃について、ロシアによるインフラ攻撃への報復だと説明しています。一方、プーチン大統領は19日、訪問先の中国・深センで記者会見し、クリミア橋はロシア軍の軍事装備品や弾薬の輸送には使っていないと主張しました。その上で、「報復する。橋への攻撃よりも、はるかに痛烈なものになる」と、ウクライナ側に警告しました。また、海上やエネルギー施設などへの攻撃停止に向けた合意について検討していたものの、今回の橋への攻撃を受け、交渉は行わないと表明しました。

title: 習氏 台湾問題で米大統領をけん制
body:
【深セン（中国広東省）＝吉永亜希子、坂本幸信】米国のトランプ大統領と中国の習近平（シージンピン）国家主席は１９日、深センで行われたアジア太平洋経済協力会議（ＡＰＥＣ）首脳会議に合わせて首脳会談を行った。両首脳は、米中の「建設的戦略安定関係」について、行動計画の策定に入ることで合意した。習氏は台湾問題に米国が関与しないよう求めたとみられる。【データ比較】空母化した護衛艦「かが」を米「ロナルド・レーガン」、中国「山東」と比べると
両首脳の会談は今年３回目。会談の冒頭、トランプ氏が「私と習氏は良好な個人的関係を築いてきた」と強調するなど、双方が融和ムードを演出した。
「建設的戦略安定関係」は５月の北京での会談で合意した。策定を進める行動計画では、経済や安全保障など幅広い分野での具体的な協力内容を明記するとみられる。
台湾問題については、習氏は「米国は正しい行動を堅持し、中米関係に大きな波乱が生じることを避けるべきだ」とトランプ氏をけん制した。台湾への武器売却計画の延期や中止を求めたものとみられる。
習氏は過去２回のトランプ氏との会談でも、「核心的利益」と位置づける台湾問題を取り上げた。中国側には、トランプ氏から「台湾独立」に「反対する」との文言を引き出す思惑があるとみられる。中国外務省の発表によると、トランプ氏は今回の会談では「『台湾独立』を支持しない」と述べ、歴代の米政権の立場を維持した。
会談では、両国が激しい競争を繰り広げる人工知能（ＡＩ）についても協議した。習氏は「ＡＩが人間の管理下に置かれるよう連携を強化すべきだ」と強調した。イラン情勢やホルムズ海峡の安全航行についても協議した可能性がある。
来年１月に期限を迎える「貿易戦争」の休戦延長に関する協議は、１２月に予定される今年４回目の会談に持ち越された。トランプ氏は「我が国の農家のために、さらなる協力を求めるつもりだ」と述べ、農産物の追加購入を中国に求めた。
一方、米半導体大手エヌビディアのジェンスン・フアン前最高経営責任者（ＣＥＯ）を巡る中国のスパイ疑惑については、メディアの前では提起されなかった。トランプ氏は会談に先立って行われた米ＦＯＸニュースのインタビューで、「我々は中国を対象にスパイ活動をするし、彼らは我々を対象としている」と述べ、問題視しない意向を示唆していた。

title: 米中露首脳「平和宣言」を発表
body: 【AFP＝時事】中国、米国、ロシアは19日、中国で史上初の3者首脳会談を行った後、「平和宣言」を発表した。ロシア大統領府（クレムリン）と中国国営メディアが伝えた。【写真】円卓を囲んで会談する米中ロ首脳広東省深センでの会談後に発表された共同声明は、「3首脳は現在の国際情勢について踏み込んだ意見交換を行い、戦略的安定と国際安全保障を維持することを約束した」としている。また3か国は、国連（UN）が世界的な課題により効果的に対処し、国際平和と安全の維持という基本的使命を果たせるよう、「国連改革の推進に取り組む」と表明した。中国国営メディアは、3か国が「国家の同意の原則と、政府当局者が享有する外交上の免責を尊重することの極めて重要な意義を認めた」と伝えた。また、「国際刑事裁判所（ICC）やその他の同様の機関は、管轄権を乱用してはならない」との認識で一致した。【翻訳編集】 AFPBB News

title: 3カ国会談 中露は「戦勝国」強調
body: 米中露3人の首脳による発言のポイントについて、現地からFNNワシントン支局・林英美記者が中継でお伝えします。【画像】握手をする高市総理と習主席の表情を見る各首脳は冒頭発言で、いずれも用意した原稿に目を通しながら、世界の平和と安定に対する重要性を強調しました。最初に発言した習近平国家主席は、「大国には特別な責任がある」と述べ、第2次大戦で3カ国が肩を並べて戦った歴史を強調しました。続くプーチン大統領も、3カ国は第2次大戦の戦勝国で、世界の平和を守る責任を共に担っていると訴えました。2人がそろって戦勝国としての結び付きを強調したことは、日本を意識した発言とも受け取れます。一方、トランプ大統領は「歴史的な会談だ」と何度も繰り返し、外交成果を強調するとともに、3カ国には世界の重要課題について対話する特別な責任があると述べました。習近平国家主席は今回の会談を踏まえ、「3カ国のハイレベルな定期的な交流の維持」を提案しています。今後、この会談が枠組みとして継続していくのかも注目されます。

title: ロヒンギャ巡る判決 内容精査と米
body:
【ワシントン共同】米国務省の報道担当者は19日、国際司法裁判所（ICJ）がミャンマーによるイスラム教徒少数民族ロヒンギャ迫害をジェノサイド（集団殺害）と認定する判決を出したことを受け「内容を精査している」と述べた。評価を留保した形。トランプ政権は、国際司法機関の判断の影響を警戒する姿勢が目立っている。【写真】ビル・ゲイツ氏が暴露したトランプ氏の「無知さ」　18年記事
報道担当者は、国連が1948年に採択した「ジェノサイド条約」について、適切な解釈が重要だと指摘。「ICJの政治利用を防ぐことも同様に重要だ」と主張した。バイデン前政権は2022年、ミャンマー国軍のロヒンギャに対する暴力をジェノサイドに当たると認定していた。

title: アンソロピック 初日終値約97ドル
body: 米国のAI（人工知能）大手アンソロピックは19日、主要なAIモデルの開発企業として初めて、ナスダック市場に新規上場した。今後の市場を占う試金石とされてきたが、公開価格を約17%上回り、97.17ドルで初日の取引を終えた。アンソロピックに求められる「指数関数的な成長」　逆風下の上場初値は、公開価格より3割以上高い、111.50ドルだった。一時、時価総額が2兆ドル（約320兆円）を超える場面もあった。今回の新規株式公開（IPO）にあたり、18日に設定した公開価格は、1株あたり83ドルだった。AI関連株を巡っては、巨額の先行投資による財務状況への懸念や、米国の中間選挙の結果を受けてデータセンター投資が減速するとの見方などから、大幅に下落するなど不安定な状態が続いている。今回のIPOへの期待は高く、需要も大きかった一方で、懸念も漂っていた。

title: 楽天証券の情報流出 遺憾と金融相
body: Takaya Yamaguchi［東京　２０日　ロイター］ - 片山さつき財務相兼金融相は２０日、‌楽天証券の情報漏えいを巡⁠り、同証券に対し１９日付で報告徴求命令を発出した​ことを明らかにした。顧客情報の漏えい事案‌そのものは「非常に遺憾」とし、「金融庁として非常‌に重く受け止‌めている」と述べ​た。同日午前の閣議後会見で語‌った。報告を待って顧客保護に向けた適‌切な対応​と、再発防止の徹底を求め‌る考えも示した。報告徴求を巡⁠り、片山金融相は「しっかりと確認、検証し、厳正に対応して⁠いく」と強調した。一​方、ロシ‌ア大統領令により現地子会社が同国企業の一時管理の対象⁠となたった日本たばこ⁠産業（ＪＴ）が１９日、業績修正とともに減配予⁠想を発表したことに伴う影響に‌つい⁠ては「産業投資に直ちに支​障が生じることは全くない」とした。

title: 楽天証券へ訴訟準備 1.5万人登録
body: ネット証券大手の楽天証券で最大で1572万件の顧客情報が流出した可能性がある問題で、都内の弁護士が集団訴訟を準備するウェブサイトを立ち上げました。【写真で見る】SNSで話題!品薄になっている「専用ノート」楽天証券は今月17日、社内のシステムが不正アクセスを受けて、最大で1572万口座の顧客情報が流出した可能性があると明らかにしています。楽天証券によりますと、▼およそ447万口座で氏名や生年月日、住所、金融資産額、それに年収などの情報と、▼およそ1125万口座で口座番号にあたる「部店・お客様コード」とログインIDの情報が漏えいした可能性があるということです。この問題を受けて、都内の弁護士が楽天証券に対する集団訴訟を準備するウェブサイトを立ち上げました。サイトを立ち上げた牧野裕貴弁護士によりますと、きょう（20日）午前中の時点で1万5000人を超える人が登録をしているということです。牧野弁護士は、「個人情報の漏えい問題は、プライバシーの問題だけにとどまらず、治安の問題になりつつある。情報を漏えいした企業の責任を追及していかなければならない」と話しています。牧野弁護士は、カーシェア大手の「タイムズカー」で不正アクセスによって免許証の画像を含む個人情報およそ660万件が流出した問題でも、運営会社の「パーク24」などへの集団提訴を呼びかけるウェブサイトを立ち上げ、訴訟に向けた準備を進めています。

title: 楽天証券に対し集団訴訟の動き
body: 楽天証券が2026年11月17日に発表した、不正アクセスによる利用者情報の漏えい問題をめぐり、集団訴訟の動きが起きている。発起人の弁護士によると、18日18時頃に参加希望者の募集を開始してから1日で約6000人の登録があったという。実際に提訴するかどうかは希望者数や楽天証券側の対応次第で検討するものの、自身の気持ちとしては提訴に傾いているとし、「『許せない』という人は泣き寝入りせずに一緒に戦ってほしい」と呼びかけた。【画像】最大約447万口座では年収・金融資産も漏えい可能性…楽天証券が明かした事実■「かなり高い確率で提訴しようという気持ち」楽天証券によると、テスト環境のシステム内で管理していた顧客情報を含む情報が外部へ流出した。最大約1125万口座で、楽天証券の部店・お客様コード、ログインIDが漏えいした可能性がある。別の最大約447万口座では、これらの情報に加え、氏名、住所、電話番号、メールアドレス、勤務先、出金先口座、利用者が申請した年収・金融資産などが漏えいした可能性があるという。なお、対象となる口座には、退会した会員のものも含まれる。また、いずれも楽天証券のログインに必要なパスワードや取引に必要な暗証番号は含まれないという。Xでは、テスト環境で個人情報を扱っていたことへの批判や、氏名や住所と年収・金融資産情報がセットで漏えいした可能性があることに対する不安の声が書き込まれている。こうしたなか、11月18日に牧野法律事務所の牧野裕貴弁護士は、楽天証券への集団訴訟の準備をしていると発表。参加希望者の登録受付を開始した。牧野弁護士は、タイムズカーの情報漏えい事案でも集団訴訟に取り組んでいる。牧野弁護士は19日にJ-CASTニュースの取材に応じ、1日で約6000人の参加希望者が集まっていると明かした。実際に提訴するかどうかは、希望者の応募状況や楽天証券側の対応により検討する。牧野弁護士は「重大な問題だと思うので、かなり高い確率でやろう（提訴しよう）という気持ち」と話した。

title: Anthropic becomes one of world's most valuable public companies in stock market debut
summary: Anthropic is the first purely AI company to be publicly listed, creating a test for the entire industry.
body:
Watch: How did Anthropic's stock market debut unfold?
Anthropic has become one of the most valuable public companies in the world after its shares began trading on the stock market, taking its valuation to roughly $1.76 trillion (£1.34 trillion).
The artificial intelligence (AI) company's Thursday debut on the Nasdaq stock exchange was a crucial test for the industry, given the huge amount of money being poured into advancing the technology.
Anthropic's shares flew past its allocation price of$83 each, showing there was plenty of excitement around AI.
Yet the company, which is behind AI chatbot Claude, will remain under intense scrutiny in the months ahead to answer the key question surrounding AI: is it all worth it?
In just a few hours of trading, Anthropic's stock seemed to show that investors remain uncertain of where exactly AI is heading. The share price rose immediately to $111.53, sending the company's market value to almost $2 trillion, before falling by the end of the day as the shares closed at $97.17.
Some investors said Anthropic's debut seemed to be a success, as shares rose roughly 17% during the day, but the broader tech market did not perform as well.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index closed down nearly 2.3%. Stocks fell in the largest tech firms, including Google's parent company Alphabet, which was down by 2.9%, while Amazon lost almost 3.9%.
The buildout happening around this era of AI is among the most expensive endeavours in the history of technology, with more than $1 trillion being spent in the last year alone by a handful of major tech companies.
The speed at which investment has grown has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble.
"Bubbles don't burst on the day of the largest deal," Richard Whittle, an economist with the University of Salford said. "They burst later, if the positive future becomes suspect."
Anthropic has made one of the fastest trips from start up to IPO in history
While the basics of the technology have been around for decades, the more recent advent of more powerful computers and related components have allowed the processing of more data than ever.
The result has been AI chatbots that simulate human speech and operate tasks like software coding, digital image generation, and searching the internet more quickly.
It represents a new way of using computers that has led to the rapid rise of Anthropic, which started just five years ago and is best known as the maker of the popular AI chatbot Claude.
As the first purely AI company to go public, Anthropic will almost certainly see significant swings in price on the stock market going forward, according to Ben Barringer, who leads technology research at Quilter Cheviot.
The "initial exuberance" will wear off, Barringer said, pointing to what happened with SpaceX earlier this year.
That company, led by Elon Musk, saw shares jump by about 10% on the first day of trading, taking the company to a record-breaking valuation of $2.2 trillion.
Within a month shares had fallen below their debut price, and have mostly fallen further since.
Most tech companies see their shares fall after hitting the stock market, often after reporting quarterly results for the first time.
But many such companies, including Meta, Amazon and Google, have gone on to become the largest and most profitable corporations in the world.
With Anthropic, investors are not only looking at a notable tech company with a major valuation, and a potentially big future in business, but a company that is the first of its kind on the stock market.
"There's no obvious peer to compare it to," Neil Wilson, an investor strategist at Saxo UK, said.
Simon Jack: Can Anthropic's record-breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting?
So, as individual investors and even researchers and investors at large funds ask themselves if Anthropic is really worth more than $1.7 trillion, or even more, there will be few answers available.
"We'll have a stab at it," Wilson said. "I don't think anyone really knows."
A few things will likely impact the company's success on the stock market in the near-term.
One of those things is the prospect of new laws governing the use of AI tools. In the US, where Anthropic is based, Democrats will be in many more positions of power come 2027, and several politicians have already said they will be looking to ensure AI tools are safe and have some guardrails attached.
Such regulation is currently unlikely at the federal level. US President Donald Trump on Thursday spoke about AI during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China, alongside Chinese and Russian counterparts, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.
Trump reiterated his position against "any form of robust regulation" around the technology, adding, "we won't allow that to happen, frankly."
The same day, however, a bipartisan group of US lawmakers formed the House AI Safety and Innovation Caucus, which will work specifically on AI regulation and safety considerations.
A significant driver of this kind of scrutiny is Anthropic itself. Company executives, including co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei, have been outspoken in their purported fears that future AI tools will become so capable they will outsmart humans, to the point where extinction is possible.
Anthropic has always put itself forward in public as an AI company that takes the safety of its technology very seriously.
Daniela Amodei, Anthropic's president and sister of Dario Amodei, boasted on Thursday that the company "had an AI safety team before we launched our first product".
"AI carries real risks," she added.
Despite the company's claims that the technology it is building at a rapid pace could be dangerous, Anthropic has made one of the quickest trips from start-up to IPO in history.
Anthropic raises $81bn in record-breaking stock market debut

title: 'I tell my son it's just fireworks': People inside besieged Yemeni city speak to BBC
summary: Orla Guerin speaks to seven people trapped in Taiz by the Houthis who reveal what life is like under siege.
body:
Houthi attacks on Taiz have killed more than 140 civilians since August, local government officials say
In the Yemeni city of Taiz, ringed by jagged mountains and Houthi rebel fighters, Ashwaq has only one way to try to soothe her frightened child - lie.
"When my 11-year-old son hears a loud sound, I tell him, 'Don't be afraid, it's just fireworks'," she says. "I don't want him to panic, but deep down I know he is old enough to understand what is happening around him. He has lived through war for most of his life."
Taiz has long been a prize - and a front line - in Yemen's civil war.
Houthi forces tightened their grip last month, fully encircling the government-controlled city, and the population - estimated to be between 600,000 and 1 million.
Since then, Yemen's third-largest city has been cut off from the world, and its residents have been largely unheard. We reached seven people inside the city who mapped out the anatomy of the siege.
They gave detailed accounts of the Houthis' death grip on Taiz. Only a minimal amount of food can get in. Prices for staples like rice, sugar and cooking oil have doubled or even trebled. Essential supplies, like medicine, water and fuel, are dwindling.
Burning piles of rubbish are producing toxic smoke that hangs over the city
On streets that used to hum with traffic and background chatter, a silence has fallen. Schools are closed and restaurants are shuttered. Suffering is being heaped on suffering. Piles of rubbish are trapped inside the city, alongside the people. When residents try to get rid of it by burning it, there is a toxic smoke. Even the air is now a Houthi weapon.
From positions on the hills, rebel fighters - and snipers - can wage war on the city below.
Estimates for the death toll vary widely. At the Office for Siege Affairs, a local government department, they say 148 civilians have been killed by Houthi attacks since August.
Some of those we contacted in Taiz do not want to be identified because they fear for their safety. Many in the city are reluctant to even speak on the phone because the Houthis control key mobile carriers.
"Sometimes it feels like the city has become a huge prison," says Ashwaq, a teacher and mother of three, who only wanted her first name to be used. She yearns for the old Taiz.
"It used to be a lively city," she says. "People loved life, worked hard, visited one another, and had hopes for the future, despite all the difficulties. Now, we hardly go out anymore. The [Houthi] shelling can happen any time, and sniper fire near the front lines makes even a short trip dangerous."
She keeps her son and two elder daughters indoors.
"I worry about them every single day, every hour, and honestly every minute," she says.
Taiz has been a major battleground in Yemen's civil war for more than a decade
War is not new to Taiz. The strategic city is the gateway to Aden - the temporary seat of the internationally recognised government - and to southern Yemen.
Houthi rebels - backed by Iran - reached the outskirts of Taiz in 2015, cutting off roads, and laying siege from three sides. A year earlier, they had seized Yemen's capital, Sanaa.
More than a decade on, the government, which is weak and fractured, has been unable to reclaim the capital and much of north-western Yemen. That's despite the backing of Saudi Arabia, and its air strikes.
In recent months, the conflict has flared up and expanded after a four-year lull. The Houthis made a lightning advance, taking territory from the government, and striking Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones.
A long-running civil war has become a threat to regional stability.
In Taiz, it is a threat to survival.
An emergency room doctor, whom we are calling Yaser, bears witness to that.
Among the war wounded recently brought to his hospital were four children, shot by Houthi snipers. They usually aim for the head and chest, he tells us. Two of the four children died.
The hardest thing he faces, as a father himself, is treating wounded children. "I have to rise to the responsibility, compose myself and support the families," he says. "It's a difficult situation that I cannot even put into words, when I see a father looking at his badly wounded child right in front of him."
Most of the injured are victims of shelling. Reaching the hospital can be an ordeal. Some families have to walk for hours from outlying areas.
They arrive exhausted, like the doctors who will treat them, and who are struggling with "everything", says Yaser. Even sterilising fluid for surgical instruments is in short supply.
He tells us the hospital is running on empty, and can carry on for two more weeks, "maybe".
Taiz's hospitals have lost 70% of their capacity and 120 health centres have closed, its governor says
If the emergency rooms are busy, so are the graveyards.
"Funerals heading to the cemeteries have become the defining scene in Taiz, around the clock," says Taiz's Governor, Nabil Shamsan.
It's not just bombs and bullets that kill, he tells us.
"The people of Taiz are losing their lives due to supply shortages, lack of food, and loss of income," he says. "Every single day, we bury dozens of Taiz residents."
He remains inside the city, and inside the siege. "I live among my people," he says.
On a video call, he looks weary but delivers a lengthy chronicle of a city being starved of oxygen - literally.
He tells us that hospitals have lost 70% of their capacity, and 120 health centres have closed. Diseases are spreading, neonatal deaths have increased, and malnutrition is surging. Hundreds of kidney patients are not getting dialysis because they can't get to hospitals or because fuel is short when they do.
The Houthi leader, Abdul Malik al-Houthi, has denied Taiz is besieged. Late last month, he claimed that routes remained open for food, medicine and humanitarian aid.
That is denied by the government, residents of Taiz, aid agencies and the United Nations.
What's at stake in the battle for the city is more than territory, says Shamsan.
He says the Houthis - who mostly follow a branch of Shia Islam - want to change the character of this predominantly Sunni city, long known as a seat of learning and a bastion of resistance.
"Everyone knows that Taiz is a hub of culture, a city characterised by freedom, political pluralism and all forms of civic life," he says. In sharp contrast, he says, the Houthis aim to impose their strict religious doctrine and drag the city "back to the dark ages".
Whatever the pressure on the city and its people, the governor insists the Houthis will never win.
How long can the city hold out, I ask.
"Until the population perishes," he replies.
Essential supplies, like medicine, water and fuel, are dwindling
Many in Taiz are resisting.
They are defending their city, alongside relatives, friends, neighbours, and five brigades of pro-government troops, who can't do the job on their own.
They don't have heavy weapons or enough numbers for the expanding front line.
Training camps have sprung up for volunteers, but the lessons can be as brief as a day or two before they are sent to join the fight.
Akram (not his real name) is already a veteran. He's 31, with a child on the way.
When Taiz was fully encircled before, in 2015, he broke away from his studies and took up arms. In that round of fighting, the Houthis gained control of his district on the outskirts, and he was uprooted. He hasn't seen his old home since then.
Last month, when Taiz was completely cut off once again, he bought a rifle, paying about $1,200 (£910) for a Chinese version of a Kalashnikov. It used to cost less than half that sum.
He tells us this fight is different to 2015.
"This time the Houthis have new technology and new missiles," he says. "They can wage a war in the air with drones. We fear the death of our families and our civilians, and ourselves."
He has already lost four friends in the past month, who left behind wives and children.
But Akram, and many others, see defending Taiz as their duty. He says that "all the sons of Taiz" will fight the Houthis "and their extremism".
The armed group is currently designated as a foreign terrorist organisation by the US (which has gone back and forth on the issue) but not by the UK or the European Union.
"They say God gave them the right to rule everyone in Yemen. We don't accept that," says Akram. "We live in freedom. We cannot surrender; we cannot leave. We cannot breathe without our city."
Almost 350,000 people have been displaced by the fighting in recent months
But it can be suffocating inside Taiz, where nightfall brings no rest.
"Every night we have bombing and shelling," says Ahmad Al-Basha, a photographer. "I think the Houthis prefer to fight at night. Maybe they don't want us and our children to sleep inside our homes."
The people of Taiz feel let down, he tells us, by their government and by the international community. "We feel frustrated and sad," he says, "because we don't see any move to help us."
Many believe the Houthis will keep a chokehold on Taiz from the outside, and exert significant control over the city without trying to enter it.
But could they fight their way in?
Ahmad believes it won't come to that but fears the worst if it does.
"Maybe they will clean Taiz of any resistance, kill people and settle scores with anyone who is against them," he says.
His greatest concern is for his children, who cannot escape the sounds of war.
Like Ashwaq, the teacher, he tries to explain it away.
"I tell them it's a party," he says, "and if it's really loud, I say it's a big party."
As Taiz endures bombing, shelling, and a sense of abandonment laced with growing hunger, Ashwaq has a parent's plea for the international community.
"Please don't forget Taiz," she says. "We are ordinary families. We want our children to study, play and dream like other children around the world. We are not just numbers in news reports."
Additional reporting by Wietske Burema and Albaraa Mansoor

title: Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya minority, top UN court rules
summary: The unprecedented International Court of Justice verdict concerns a 2017 military crackdown that killed thousands.
body:
Rohingya genocide: What was said in court and what happens now?
Myanmar has been found guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority by the International Court of Justice (ICJ).
The verdict marks the first time a state has ever been found to have committed genocide by an international court.
Yuji Iwasawa, president of the UN's top court, said Myanmar had the "intention to destroy" a substantial part of the Rohingya population and engaged in "extensive destruction of evidence" to hide its crimes.
A military crackdown in 2017 killed thousands of Rohingya and forced more than 700,000 to flee Buddhist-majority Myanmar, formerly known as Burma. Myanmar denied the claims against it, saying its forces had responded to attacks by armed groups.
Bowen: Myanmar genocide verdict is historic and could have far-reaching implications
Rohingyas at the Cox's Bazar camp in Bangladesh, where around a million refugees now reside, watched the verdict live
The court found on Thursday that "genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence" it had seen.
The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world. The ICJ also found in favour by majority that Myanmar had violated several other parts of the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The case brought by The Gambia centred around so-called "clearance operations" initiated in 2017 in Rakhine State, where many of the Rohingya Muslim minority resided.
After fighters from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (Arsa) launched deadly attacks on more than 30 police posts there, Myanmar troops, backed by local Buddhist mobs, launched a wave of violence, prompting a mass exodus of Rohingya.
Refugees recounted entire villages being burned down and the mass killing of civilians, while numerous survivors and eyewitnesses provided testimony that the Myanmar military had also raped and abused Rohingya women and girls.
The ICJ determined that around 10,000 Rohingya were "violently killed" during the clearance operation, while more than 700,000 are thought to have fled to Bangladesh by foot or by sea. The court found that approximately 815,000 had been targeted in some way.
Watch: Genocide judgement will 'mean a great deal' for Rohingya community
Iwasawa said Myanmar's military engaged in "indiscriminate" killings, the execution of men, "widespread" sexual violence, "extreme violence" against children and the deliberate burning of Rohingya homes.
He said the military had also attacked Rohingya as they were fleeing to Bangladesh.
Myanmar, he added, had engaged in "extensive destruction of evidence" by burning or disposing of bodies, burned and bulldozed sites that were cleared and failed to prosecute those who had perpetrated the acts of violence.
While the ICJ recognised the role Arsa played, it found there was "overlap" between an "anti-Rohingya hate speech campaign" - which portrayed the Rohingya as "sub-human" and "a violent threat" - and the clearance operations that made violence against the population more likely.
Myanmar consistently denied genocide against the Rohingya, saying its operations had targeted militant or insurgent threats in response to the Arsa attacks.
In January, government representative Ko Ko Hlaing told the ICJ that the country "was not obliged to remain idle and allow terrorists to have free reign". He said he had "no comment" following Thursday's verdict.
The ICJ also looked at the wider treatment of Rohingya leading up to the clearance operation and found that policies like limiting married couples to two children were discriminatory and aimed to erode their rights.
It said Myanmar had an obligation to pay proportionate reparations, but said an exact figure could be determined at a later date.
The court's decision was welcomed by Rohingya communities and human rights groups.
"This is like formal recognition of our suffering," says Mohammed Nowkim, a Rohingya who was driven out of Rakhine in 2017 and now lives in Canada. "The Rohingya have been waiting for justice for decades."
Human Rights Watch said the ruling was "long-awaited recognition of the suffering the Rohingya have endured".
Meanwhile, UN human rights chief Volker Türk said the "suffering, misery and humiliation" inflicted on the Rohingya people was a "stain on the conscience of humanity". He added that the court's decision "must now translate into real action".
To implicate the Myanmar government in genocide, the court had to determine not just that terrible acts had been committed, but that there was an intent on the part of officials or arms of the state to partially or completely destroy the group.
Thursday's ruling is without precedent. Myanmar now carries the stain of being the first state to have been found to have violated the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The ICJ has only twice before ruled on claims of state-backed genocide in the years since the Genocide Convention was signed in the aftermath of the Holocaust, in both cases finding there was insufficient evidence to attribute the actions to the state.
Dozens of individuals have been found guilty of genocide, but finding their actions were at the direct behest of the state requires a higher evidential bar to prove genocide, the gravest of crimes under international law.
Rohingya refugees were seen reacting as the ICJ verdict was broadcast on a big screen in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh
Philippe Sands KC, a top human rights lawyer who helped bring the case, described it as an "historic judgment".
He told BBC Radio 4's World at One programme that it was "right up there with the great moments of international justice: Nuremberg, Pinochet, and others", referring to the trials of Nazi leaders following World War Two and that of the Chilean dictator, respectively.
However, the ICJ is not a criminal court and its powers of enforcement are limited. It cannot send military officials to prison, while it relies on the UN Security Council and political pressure to impose its rulings.
The ruling will, though, have implications for other genocide cases pending with the ICJ, including one brought by South Africa against Israel over its war in Gaza.
Sands said that pending case had been the "elephant in the room" during the Myanmar hearings.
He added that, while ruling against Myanmar did not mean the court would find similarly with Gaza, if it had not found Myanmar responsible, the case against Israel "would, in effect, be over". Israel says the case against it is "wholly unfounded".
ICJ president Yuji Iwasawa said Myanmar had the "intention to destroy" a substantial part of the Rohingya population
Antonia Mulvey, executive director of Legal Action Worldwide, told the BBC that the court had not accepted Myanmar's counter-terrorism defence and had found for the first time that rape and sexual violence was an act of genocide, positions it would bear in mind for future cases.
A spokesperson for the US State Department said "the proper interpretation" of the Genocide Convention is of "paramount importance", and so is "preventing politicisation" of the International Criminal Court. "We are studying the decision to fully assess its implications," they said.
They said they share the "grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights against Rohingya Muslims and members of other minority groups", and added the US is the "leading donor for the Rohingya refugee humanitarian response".
Following Thursday's ruling, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the government was ordering Myanmar's defence attaché be expelled and that he was summoning its charge d'affaires.
He pledged to set out "further action in the coming days to ensure those responsible are held to account" after a cross-party group of MPs called for the government to resume sanctions against Myanmar's military.
Myanmar faces historic genocide verdict at UN court over Rohingya massacres
Millions opposed military rule in Myanmar. Is their dream of a revolution over?
Rohingya refugees face fierce new wave of hostility in Malaysia

title: Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say
summary: European allies of Ukraine say they have a "united" negotiating position at a summit in Berlin.
body:
European leaders have said they are ready for negotiations with Russia on ending the war in Ukraine, in a strong show of support for Kyiv.
"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".
They were speaking at Berlin's summit of Ukraine's allies known as the Coalition of the Willing.
Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side". Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks.
Trump had earlierheld historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, south-eastern China, with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping and later dialled into the Berlin summit from Air Force One.
In a lengthy press conference following his talks with Trump and Xi, Putin addressed the question of multilateral peace talks, saying the Americans were "insistently" asking Russia to allow the Europeans to take part.
Putin claimed Russia was not against the idea but said Moscow wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".
"That is why, through diplomatic channels, we have invited the Europeans to come to Moscow in order to determine their positions. And after that, we will decide in what format we will continue the dialogue with Ukraine."
But Putin also said that "every day" Russia heard that European leaders were talking about war coming in 2030. "But we are not planning to attack anyone... Is that normal? I do not think so," he said. Still, Putin added, Russia understood that "discussing issues linked to security in Europe is pointless without the Europeans".
Jared Kushner told reporters that the US president had come away from Shenzhen believing that "peace is achievable".
Striking an upbeat note, Kushner said that the Russians were willing to trust the instinct of the US envoys "on our behalf" that the Europeans should be at the table and that Moscow was now "comfortable" with Ukraine having security guarantees based on the idea enshrined in Nato's Article Five that requires allies to come to a country's defence if it comes under attack.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who also was at the summit in Germany's capital, has long sought a guarantee equivalent to Nato's collective defence clause, and there has been little indication that Putin would accept that kind of condition.
Russia rejects outright the idea of Ukrainian membership of Nato, but reports say US negotiators have mulled the idea of giving Kyiv Article Five-style guarantees without being part of the Western defensive alliance if it agrees to painful territorial concessions.
Zelensky and the three European leaders – Merz, Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron – were not as upbeat as Kushner, and the Ukrainian president made clear that the Russian president had spurned every proposal so far: "Putin has always said no."
The German chancellor was equally sceptical, although he said with US involvement the chance of peace was increasing. Europe was willing to enter "serious discussions on European security" with Russia, he explained, "as long as it's matched with a serious discussion and only first a peace agreement with Ukraine".
"These talks have to begin, and we will accept if conditions are acceptable for Europe and Ukraine," said Merz.
He also said any attempts to divide Europe into spheres of influence run by major powers was unacceptable, amid concerns on the continent that this issue may have been on the agenda at the trilateral talks in Shenzhen.
Analysis: Trilateral summit high on spectacle, short on substance
"A 'Yalta format' will not bring peace," Merz said, referring to the post-World War Two agreement between the US, the USSR and Britain in 1945.
He also sought to downplay the Shenzhen summit as above all "a photo opportunity."
"The US understands that there can be no peace without us. We, in turn, know that with the United States by our side, the prospects for peace increase," Merz added.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk also took exception to Trump's description of Putin as a "friend" at the Shenzhen summit, saying:  "Mr Putin is not our friend and will never be."
Meanwhile, Macron urged Ukraine's allies to do the "maximum" to deliver the much-needed air defence systems Kyiv needed to repel deadly Russian attacks.
The French leader also urged the allies to "reopen the question" of Ukraine's membership in Nato.
There have been mixed messages from Moscow on European participation to the talks. Last week, following a visit to Moscow, the US envoys, Steve Witkoff and Kushner, appeared certain that Europe would soon have a seat at the negotiating table.
But the Russians were more circumspect and this week Putin's aide Yury Ushakov said a "great deal" would have to be done before the format could be expanded, suggesting that several more rounds of discussions would have to be held before any four-sided talks could take place.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Several buildings were damaged in the latest Russian attack on Ukraine's capital Kyiv
While Russia has engaged with several rounds of talks over the last year, little in Moscow's rhetoric or actions suggests that the Kremlin is considering scaling down its war on Ukraine.
It continues to pound Kyiv's energy infrastructure to cripple it as winter takes hold, increasing numbers of civilian casualties are being recorded across the country, and Kremlin officials have not budged from Russia's demands for Ukrainian sovereign territory.
As delegations were meeting in China and Germany on Thursday, several buildings in Kyiv's historic centre came under attack from drones. One person was killed in a strike on a residential building in the Podilskyi neighbourhood, while the Dutch and Austrian embassies as well as Saint Volodymyr's Cathedral reported damage.
And Putin also vowed that Moscow's response to a Ukrainian strike on the Crimean Bridge linking Russia with occupied Crimea would be "considerably more painful" than what Kyiv had achieved.
He also said he had discussed a "possible ceasefire in a number of areas" but had decided against it after the attack on the bridge.
Still, Putin claimed to be "interested" in ending the war and was ready to make compromises, while Ukraine and Europe were not.
"I assure you, we have no desire at all to continue this armed conflict," Putin said, despite the fact that Russia has in recent months intensified its attacks on Ukraine's critical infrastructure as cold winter approaches.
Kyiv and its European allies say that – in the absence of any major success on the vast front line – the Kremlin leader is seeking to break Ukrainian resistance by leaving millions of civilians without electricity and water supply.

title: Trump, Putin and Xi release 'peace declaration' after historic meeting
summary: While the presidents have previously met for one-on-one meetings, this is their first trilateral discussion.
body:
Watch: What did Trump, Xi and Putin get out of their historic meeting?
US President Donald Trump and his Russian and Chinese counterparts Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping have issued a "joint declaration of peace" following historic trilateral talks.
The three leaders met for 90 minutes in China's south-eastern city of Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.
While the presidents have previously had one-on-one meetings, these are their first trilateral talks.
In the declaration, they said "nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought" and that the countries planned to increase the production and supply of petroleum. They also said they were "committed to reform the UN" to respond more effectively to global challenges.
Thursday's statement also flagged the issue of immunity enjoyed by state officials and said "they agreed that the International Criminal Court and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction".
Trump praised the trilateral meeting calling it "a great and highly consequential trip", in a social media post while flying back to Washington on Air Force One.
In the same post, the president announced  he would host a news conference to talk about the trip on Friday at the White House.
While in China, Trump met Putin ahead of the trilateral, in their first meeting since August 2025, where the US president greeted his Russian counterpart as his "friend".
He also spoke with Xi in a separate conversation, describing the pair's relationship as "very special".
Beyond the warmth and shared niceties, however, the three men had different goals and motivations for the sit-down.
Analysis: Trilateral summit high on spectacle, short on substance
This is a remarkable diplomatic moment for China's Xi - but it comes with pitfalls
The opening remarks of the trilateral gave some indication about what was to be discussed during the closed-door meeting.
Before giving the floor to his fellow leaders, Xi said that "positive interaction among major powers is not a matter of choice, but a mandatory requirement".
Putin followed this by highlighting a shared interest in ending the Ukraine war and said the conversation would also touch on food and energy security.
China has officially remained neutral since Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, rejecting accusations from Kyiv and its allies that it has been tacitly supporting Moscow, including by exporting dual-use technology used by the Russian military.
Beijing has also repeatedly called for negotiations and a political settlement while avoiding condemnation of Russia's aggression.
Trump greets 'my friend' Putin ahead of meeting with Xi
Meanwhile, Trump closed by saying the presidents of three of the world's largest countries have a "special responsibility" to maintain productive dialogue.
"Too often past leaders have avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements," he said, adding: "We feel the opposite."
Trump referenced the three countries' nuclear capabilities and said they are "uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth".
It is "vital" that they co-operate to "combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world", he said, adding: "That's what we're doing in Iran."
"We're not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon".
Trump then turned to Ukraine and said he and Putin have had a "long discussion" on the conflict there already.
He added that Putin "and I hope the other side, would like to see an end to that war".
Putin addressed the media following the trilateral meeting and described it as an "important chapter in the history of diplomacy".
He said Ukraine and Europe were not yet ready to make compromises to resolve the conflict in Ukraine -but he said Russia had invited EU representatives to Moscow to better understand Europe's position.
As the talks were under way in China, and even as Putin was holding his press conference claiming to be ready for peace, Ukraine's capital Kyiv was under attack from Russian drones.
Putin has repeatedly rejected all ceasefire offers from Ukraine, insisting on his maximalist demands which Kyiv and its European allies say are tantamount to de facto capitulation of Ukraine.
In Shenzhen, the Kremlin leader also vowed a"far more painful" retaliationin response to Ukrainian attacks on the bridge connecting Russia to Ukraine's occupied peninsula of Crimea. A missile and drone attack on Tuesday destroyed its central road section.
There was no mention from Putin of almost five years of Russian attacks on power plants, bridges and residential buildings in Ukraine.
The Russian president also directly addressed comparisons between his meeting with Trump and Xi and the 1945 Yalta Conference, where the leaders of the Soviet Union, Britain and the US met towards the end of World War Two.
"Nobody divided up the world at Yalta. It simply codified the realities that had emerged after WW2.
"And when it comes to today's conflicts, the realities on the ground will have to be accepted."
The three presidents spoke behind closed doors at the Kylin Villa, the exclusive resort in Shenzhen
The Kremlin released a video showing Putin leaving the summit venue and saying goodbye to Xi.
"Thank you for organising this," Putin said. "I don't think anyone even expected everything to go so well."
Meanwhile, China's president described his meeting with Putin and Trump as "positive, constructive, and highly productive", according to the country's state broadcaster CCTV.
It added that Xi recalled "the history of fighting side-by-side during WW2", as the three leaders emphasised the importance of "cherishing the hard-won peace".
Thursday's trilateral meeting was reportedly the idea of Putin.
Some Russian newspapers called it a "diplomatic victory" as after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine many Western leaders were trying to isolate him.
The summit also marked the first time since Russia's war in Ukraine began that Putin took part in an international gathering attended by leaders from countries including Canada, Japan and Australia.
Russian 'nuclear briefcase' spotted at APEC summit
US lawmakers responded with frustration to Trump's warmth towards America's geopolitical adversaries.
"I was encouraged by some of the commitments that came out of the President's meetings in Asia, particularly the recognition that nuclear war must never be fought," Republican Senator John Curtis said in an emailed statement to the BBC.
But Curtis also said he was concerned about Trump's approach to the foreign leaders, adding that "Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are not our friends".
"We should not treat them as though they share our values or interests," Curtis, who sits on the Senate foreign relations committee, added.
"Doing so risks undermining our national security, weakening trust with our allies, and sending the wrong message about where America stands."
Jeanne Shaheen, a ranking Democratic member on the same committee, chose harsher words in her comment.
"President Trump's 'friend' is a murderous war criminal," she wrote on X.
With additional reporting from Brandon Drenon

title: Anthropic becomes one of world's most valuable public companies in stock market debut
summary: Anthropic is the first purely AI company to be publicly listed, creating a test for the entire industry.
body:
Watch: How did Anthropic's stock market debut unfold?
Anthropic has become one of the most valuable public companies in the world after its shares began trading on the stock market, taking its valuation to roughly $1.76 trillion (£1.34 trillion).
The artificial intelligence (AI) company's Thursday debut on the Nasdaq stock exchange was a crucial test for the industry, given the huge amount of money being poured into advancing the technology.
Anthropic's shares flew past its allocation price of$83 each, showing there was plenty of excitement around AI.
Yet the company, which is behind AI chatbot Claude, will remain under intense scrutiny in the months ahead to answer the key question surrounding AI: is it all worth it?
In just a few hours of trading, Anthropic's stock seemed to show that investors remain uncertain of where exactly AI is heading. The share price rose immediately to $111.53, sending the company's market value to almost $2 trillion, before falling by the end of the day as the shares closed at $97.17.
Some investors said Anthropic's debut seemed to be a success, as shares rose roughly 17% during the day, but the broader tech market did not perform as well.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index closed down nearly 2.3%. Stocks fell in the largest tech firms, including Google's parent company Alphabet, which was down by 2.9%, while Amazon lost almost 3.9%.
The buildout happening around this era of AI is among the most expensive endeavours in the history of technology, with more than $1 trillion being spent in the last year alone by a handful of major tech companies.
The speed at which investment has grown has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble.
"Bubbles don't burst on the day of the largest deal," Richard Whittle, an economist with the University of Salford said. "They burst later, if the positive future becomes suspect."
Anthropic has made one of the fastest trips from start up to IPO in history
While the basics of the technology have been around for decades, the more recent advent of more powerful computers and related components have allowed the processing of more data than ever.
The result has been AI chatbots that simulate human speech and operate tasks like software coding, digital image generation, and searching the internet more quickly.
It represents a new way of using computers that has led to the rapid rise of Anthropic, which started just five years ago and is best known as the maker of the popular AI chatbot Claude.
As the first purely AI company to go public, Anthropic will almost certainly see significant swings in price on the stock market going forward, according to Ben Barringer, who leads technology research at Quilter Cheviot.
The "initial exuberance" will wear off, Barringer said, pointing to what happened with SpaceX earlier this year.
That company, led by Elon Musk, saw shares jump by about 10% on the first day of trading, taking the company to a record-breaking valuation of $2.2 trillion.
Within a month shares had fallen below their debut price, and have mostly fallen further since.
Most tech companies see their shares fall after hitting the stock market, often after reporting quarterly results for the first time.
But many such companies, including Meta, Amazon and Google, have gone on to become the largest and most profitable corporations in the world.
With Anthropic, investors are not only looking at a notable tech company with a major valuation, and a potentially big future in business, but a company that is the first of its kind on the stock market.
"There's no obvious peer to compare it to," Neil Wilson, an investor strategist at Saxo UK, said.
Simon Jack: Can Anthropic's record-breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting?
So, as individual investors and even researchers and investors at large funds ask themselves if Anthropic is really worth more than $1.7 trillion, or even more, there will be few answers available.
"We'll have a stab at it," Wilson said. "I don't think anyone really knows."
A few things will likely impact the company's success on the stock market in the near-term.
One of those things is the prospect of new laws governing the use of AI tools. In the US, where Anthropic is based, Democrats will be in many more positions of power come 2027, and several politicians have already said they will be looking to ensure AI tools are safe and have some guardrails attached.
Such regulation is currently unlikely at the federal level. US President Donald Trump on Thursday spoke about AI during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China, alongside Chinese and Russian counterparts, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.
Trump reiterated his position against "any form of robust regulation" around the technology, adding, "we won't allow that to happen, frankly."
The same day, however, a bipartisan group of US lawmakers formed the House AI Safety and Innovation Caucus, which will work specifically on AI regulation and safety considerations.
A significant driver of this kind of scrutiny is Anthropic itself. Company executives, including co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei, have been outspoken in their purported fears that future AI tools will become so capable they will outsmart humans, to the point where extinction is possible.
Anthropic has always put itself forward in public as an AI company that takes the safety of its technology very seriously.
Daniela Amodei, Anthropic's president and sister of Dario Amodei, boasted on Thursday that the company "had an AI safety team before we launched our first product".
"AI carries real risks," she added.
Despite the company's claims that the technology it is building at a rapid pace could be dangerous, Anthropic has made one of the quickest trips from start-up to IPO in history.
Anthropic raises $81bn in record-breaking stock market debut

title: GTA 6 breaks records as sales top $2bn - industry estimate
summary: Rockstar Games ended a 13-year wait with what is expected to be the biggest entertainment launch ever.
body:
GTA 6 central characters Lucia and Jason
Grand Theft Auto 6 is estimated to have become the biggest entertainment release in history following the blockbuster video game's launch on Thursday, after a 13-year wait.
The highly anticipated open-world action-adventure has sold more than 24.5 million units as of Thursday, raking in about $2.36bn (£1.8bn), according to analytics platform Sensor Tower.
In comparison, this year's highest grossing movie so far, Spider-Man: Brand New Day, made$2.5bn over its entire run in cinemas.
GTA 6's maker Rockstar and parent company Take-Two have not released details of the game's sales but said demand has been "unprecedented". The BBC has contacted both the firms for comment.
GTA 6 is the latest instalment in Rockstar's nearly three decade old crime simulator franchise, which has become one of the most popular games in history.
At its core, the series is a satirical take on the American dream, putting players in the shoes of career criminals in Leonida, the game's Florida-inspired state.
The latest game follows new characters Lucia and her partner Jason, a pair of small-time criminals.
Grand Theft Auto 6 is a masterpiece, say critics
Sensor Tower said GTA 6 will be so popular that it will reduce the time gamers spend on other single-player titles by 10%.
The research firm said its estimates are based on email receipts data and other statistical sources that track millions of people daily. They also track public profiles across major gaming platforms like PlayStation and Xbox, where GTA 6 is available.
Anticipation for the blockbuster title has grown through repeated delays, following a 13-year wait.
GTA 6 has been hailed by some reviewers as one of the most impressive gaming experiences ever. Entertainment media site IGN described it as an "uncompromisingly engineered" masterpiece.
The release of GTA 6 at midnight on Thursday across various time zones saw many gamers stay up through the night, while some took the following day off to play the game.

title: California targets Nvidia in China AI chip probe
summary: The probe by California, where the AI chipmaker has its global headquarters, follows former CEO Jensen Huang's departure.
body:
California has served an investigative subpoena on the AI chip designer Nvidia in the wake of a scandal that ended in the departure of longtime CEO Jensen Huang.
The state's top law enforcement officer, attorney general Rob Bonta, said he is probing whether Nvidia or Huang's actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information, adding that such actions could violate California law if the company is found to have mislead investors and the public.
The BBC has contacted Nvidia for comment.
"Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors," Bonta said on Thursday.
How could the Nvidia CEO’s affair threaten US national security?
Nvidia has its global headquarters in Santa Clara, California.
Earlier this month, it emerged that Huang had an extramarital relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang, who was an executive at the Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed.
Some members of the US Congress have urged the Department of Commerce to investigate whether Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer, diverted Nvidia chips to China.
Megaspeed has previously said it is aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".
Nvidia shares have plummeted 22% since the New York Times reported on the affair in early November.
Earlier this week, the company's board chair Harvey Jones said Nvidia had no intention of reinstating  Jensen Huang after the longtime Nvidia boss and co-founder issued a statement saying he would be "honoured" to return, as some tech leaders including Elon Musk campaigned on his behalf.

title: Tens of thousands of UK fridges secured from hackers in secret nationwide operation
summary: Supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants and stadiums have been scrambling to make their devices safe.
body:
Sweden was among countries to report a cyber incident in which some supermarket fridge units had been hiked up in temperature
A behind the scenes cyber-security operation has taken place to secure tens of thousands of fridges and freezers at major UK supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants, petrol stations and stadiums from hackers, the BBC has learned.
Recentwaves of cyber-attacks in Europehave seen tonnes of food spoiled at hundreds of stores, causing millions of pounds of damage.
France has blamed Iran for one of the waves of attacks that impacted its supermarkets,a claim Tehran denies.
It was thought the UK hadlargely escaped such hacksas the British refrigeration industry relies on different devices but there was in fact a potential vulnerability the sector has been rushing to fix.
In late October, security researchers discovered a major flaw that, if found by hackers, could have led to even worse damage to the UK.
Since then, researchers, IT teams and the National Cyber Security Centre have been working around the clock to warn dozens of companies.
The BBC has not reported on the large-scale, secretive operation until now to reduce the chances of hackers causing harm if they found the vulnerability.
The security threat was discovered by ethical hackers at a firm called Omega Systems - it was then verified and expanded upon by experts at Pentest Partners who helped raise the alarm.
The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), the Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (Defra) and Food Standards Agency (FSA) were then involved in the campaign to plug the security holes.
They held industry conference calls and tasked teams to contact firms at risk.
Thousands of devices controlling tens of thousands of refrigeration devices were taken off the open internet either remotely, or in some cases, physically - with staff ordered to remove internet cables and monitor temperatures manually.
BBC news has learnt most major supermarkets have been forced to divert IT teams to address the risks, with a worker at one large chain saying they took hundreds of devices offline every day over the course of a week.
"It did feel like a race against time as we were expecting another wave of these fridge hacks to come," said the person, who did not want to be publicly named.
"From a business perspective it could have been potentially devastating with business interruption and supply chain problems. Our warehouses have millions of pounds worth of food that could have been spoiled if any hackers found out about this method of attack," they added.
There have been three waves of hacks on refrigeration temperature controllers so far this year:
In August, fridges at a small number of US military bases were impacted
On 11th and 12th October hundreds of supermarkets and food processing sites in France were hit when Danfoss temperature control systems were targeted
On the 1st and 2nd of November dozens of supermarkets across seven European countries were hit, with Belgium, Luxembourg the were worst affected. A small number of blood bank sites in France were also impacted
The waves of attacks prompted an expert at Omega Solutions to examine the security of the most popular refrigeration controllers in the UK, made by British firm Resource Data Management (RDM).
RDM disputes the critical nature of the vulnerabilities exposed but has been praised for its professional response to address the concerns, the BBC understands.
As well as supermarkets, multiple other areas of UK food and beverage industry were also warned to take action about the risks.
These include convenience stores, petrol stations, restaurants and fast food chains, sports arenas, hotels, food processing plants and cold storage sites.
Each RDM controller can be used to remotely control the temperature of dozens of fridges and freezers
"These popular controllers had a similar weak password problem to the Danfoss and other controllers that were attacked so successfully in previous hacks so we had to get the message out as soon as possible and keep it secret," said Ken Munro of Pen Test Partners.
"There is so much extra attention on these ubiquitous bits of kit now that it was likely a matter of days until criminals or nation state hackers figured it out," he added.
RDM, though, says comparisons with the units attacked in mainland Europe are not fair because hacking their fridges and freezers would have involved getting hold of a piece of hardware.
The ethical hackers say this would have been achievable as the hardware in question can be purchased cheaply online on sites like eBay.
"This was a vulnerability identified in a test environment," said Ged Evans, CEO of RDM.
He said the test "went beyond" what such exercises usually involved, as it "included, dismantling our hardware".
"In any event we have acted at pace to address this issue and have already deployed first patch releases and have been in proactive contact with our customers to flag any issues and recommend mitigatory steps," he added.
RDM confirmed that there is no sign of any malicious activity on the controllers and that it continues to work with the NCSC and other authorities to monitor the situation.

title: Airbnb's divisive new house rules come into force
summary: New rules on what Airbnb hosts can reasonably ask guests to do could mean fewer chores but higher costs for customers.
body:
New rules on what Airbnb hosts can reasonably ask guests to do have come into force.
Hosts should now not normally ask guests to wash up, for example, but can appeal to Airbnb if they have a compelling reason.
Some guests have found lists of house rules laborious to complete, withone telling the BBC"it was not relaxing at all".
But some hosts have said that the costs of paying for extra cleaning may have to be passed on to customers.
The new Airbnb rules,announced last month, allow hosts to choose from seven standard house rules, which include determining how many people can stay overnight, and whether or not pets or smoking are allowed.
Hosts can then set additional rules, but guests shouldn't be asked to do the washing up, remove sheets from beds, take rubbish out or avoid using utilities.
Airbnb has begun reviewing listings andwill be sending emails to hosts,external"who need to take action" it said.
Hosts can appeal to Airbnb to argue an additional house rule is necessary, and ask Airbnb to approve it.
If the house rule is not approved and the host keeps it anyway, Airbnb will flag this to guests on the host's listing page with a message such as "includes cleaning tasks".
Airbnb said chores can make customers hesitate about booking through the platform, arguing that making house rules "clearer" would increase the number of clients.
But some hosts have said they may have to pass the extra cleaning costs on to guests.
Lisa Clewes, who runs a Welsh holiday let, told the BBC she was"horrified" at the state her guests left the houseafter a dinner party.
There were broken glasses, drinks cans on the floor, pans full of food on the table and fish guts left in the garden.
Clewes said it typically takes cleaners four hours to turn around her three-bedroom property.
She said guests leaving more mess could mean hiring extra cleaners and increasing costs – expenses that may ultimately be passed on to her customers.
Airbnb host Lisa Clewes said her Welsh holiday let was left 'a complete mess' by a group of guests
The changes have come as a relief to guests like Jessica Newhook, who says she has been faced with lengthy checkout lists, often on top of hefty cleaning fees.
She booked an Airbnb in Florida for a family reunion of 11 guests and says they had to "leave the property move-in ready for the cleaners", despite paying a $250 (£187) cleaning fee.
"We had rules about everything and it was not relaxing at all," she said.
The new rules have added to growing frustration among owners following increases in Airbnb's commission rates last year.
Many are investing in their own websites and social media to attract direct bookings and avoid platform fees.
Not all hosts are concerned about the changes, however.
Matt Porsz, who hosts and manages other Airbnb properties full-time, told the BBC previously the review system encourages both hosts and guests to behave reasonably.

title: UK and EU to agree youth mobility scheme, BBC understands
summary: The scheme is expected to be approved at Friday's UK-EU summit, with new deals on food trade and carbon emissions also on the table.
body:
Watch: Channel action plan could be 'big win' out of UK-EU summit, Burnham says
Up to 100,000 young people from the EU would be allowed to travel, work and study in the UK per year under a new youth mobility scheme set to be agreed on Friday, the BBC understands.
The same number of young Britons would be allowed into Europe under the scheme, expected to be approved at the UK-EU summit in Brussels. Downing Street has not commented on the details, but said talks were "down to the wire" on Thursday.
The prime minister has said a "Channel action plan" on immigration could also be struck, while negotiators are seeking agreements on food trade rules and carbon emissions pricing.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has accused Andy Burnham of "reopening the divisions" of the Brexit referendum.
A new youth mobility scheme would aim to make it easier for young people to work and travel both in the EU and UK.
The UK already has schemes in place with 13 non-EU countries including Australia, Canada and India.
In 2024, the EU proposed allowing 18 to 30 year-olds to work or study in the EU and UK for up to four years.
Labour, which was then in opposition, rejected the deal - arguing it amounted to reinstating freedom of movement.
Since coming to government, the party has suggested it would consider a more restricted scheme with a time limit, a cap on the numbers coming to the UK and a ban on participants from claiming benefits.
The UK's request to limit numbers has proved to be a sticking point in negotiation ahead of the summit, along with the EU's request that EU students should pay the same tuition fees at UK universities as domestic students.
Speaking to broadcasters on Thursday evening, Burnham was asked if there were any circumstances in which the UK would walk away from a deal on Friday.
"There would always be those circumstances because I'm in this to get the best deal for Britain, always," he said.
"But what's in it for us is the possibility of lower food prices and I can't turn my back on that, lower costs for business, cutting red tape, and a really big win potentially of more collaboration on immigration - a Channel action plan - which is a really big deal if we can land that tomorrow.
"So I hope people can understand why I have pushed this because it could be a really good deal for Britain."
Burnham previously said the UK and EU could link up their law enforcement efforts, including sharing more data and criminal records of foreign nationals.
The prime minister's spokesman has said if a deal were secured, the government would introduce legislation to Parliament next week to implement changes.
The Brexit debate is back – and there are nerves about what happens next
Faisal Islam: What's in the Brexit reset food deal and are there trade-offs?
The EU that Burnham is eyeing up is very different to the one Britain left
An agreement on trade could remove checks and paperwork faced by food companies exporting to the EU.
The government argues this could add £5bn to the economy and cut food prices.
However, it could mean the UK will have to follow certain EU rules on products, for example on gene-edited crops or labelling.
Burnham has also said the summit would allow the UK to raise concernsabout the Made in Europe scheme,which is designed to protect industries from unfair Chinese competition.
Speaking to the BBC's Today programme on Thursday, Badenoch said she wanted to see easier trading with the EU, but "not trade at any cost".
She also said the new deals could see UK companies having to follow EU rules, even those that do not trade with the bloc.
Burnham has previously suggested he could commit Labour to building a closer long-term future relationship with Europe, including asking to rejoin the organisation as a full member - however, he has ruled out major changes before the next election.
The party's 2024 manifesto promised not to return to the EU, the single market, customs union or freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to live and work elsewhere in the bloc without a visa.
Earlier this week, former deputy prime minister David Lammy urged the prime minister to go into the next general election promising to rejoin the EU.
However, the subjecthas divided his cabinetwith one minister warning of the costs that would come with reversing Brexit.
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage,speaking to The Sun,external, said he does "not believe for a minute" the country would "ever vote to rejoin" the EU.
He added: "I think what Burnham is doing is playing a very cynical political game. He's trying to pick up votes from the Lib Dems, pick up votes from the Greens, and using it as a massive distraction from all the problems that he can't deal with."

title: The Brexit debate is back – and there are nerves about what happens next
summary: Many of the names and arguments that defined the Brexit period are emerging again, as the debate over the UK being part of the EU is back on the agenda.
body:
"Stop Me If You Think You've Heard This One Before" sang Morrissey, as part of The Smiths in 1987, shortly before the band's acrimonious divorce.
It's a lyric Brexit veterans might be humming to themselves this week. Maybe even the prime minister, who is an avid fan of the Manchester band.
Some of the names - and arguments - that defined the Brexit period inside and outside Parliament are starting to emerge again, as the debate about the UK's relationship with the EU returns.
"It's like déjà vu with knobs on," said one veteran of the Leave campaign to us.
A new group called Stay Out has been set up, backed by figures who were part of the official Leave campaign in 2016. Boris Johnson has been back in the headlines, saying he still thinks Britons would choose to be outside the bloc.
Pro-EU groups such as the European Movement are raising their voices, pointing to the range of politicians, diplomats and academics they have supporting their argument. And a steady stream of Labour figures are now emerging to say they want to rejoin.
The former Deputy Prime Minister David Lammymade the argument on the BBC on Wednesday, saying Labour should go into the next election backing renegotiating membership of the EU and then putting that to people in another referendum.
He joins a list of cabinet ministers under Sir Keir Starmer who want to revisit EU membership; a list that includes former Chancellor Rachel Reeves, former Business Secretary Peter Kyle and former Welsh Secretary Jo Stevens. Others who served around Sir Keir's cabinet table think the same privately.
That is significant. Yes, they all backed Remain in 2016. But these are figures who were part of a government elected on a manifesto saying it was important to make Brexit work.
They set red lines in that manifesto because they thought the public had moved on. But they have now decided to say - most of them very publicly - that they think the picture has changed and the UK needs to think again.
The prime minister has opened the door to all options, from single market membership to rejoining the customs union to a referendum on full membership.
But in recent days, his language has softened a little from the clear commitment in his party conference speech that around the time of this Friday's summit he would "lay out to the country" the different options for Britain's long-term relationship with Brussels.
After some confusion about when this would take place, the government now says this will happen around the time that Burnham presents his 10-year plan, right before Parliament's Christmas break.
Burnham's allies say this will allow him to tie his EU policy more closely to his domestic agenda, arguing that a different arrangement with Europe would help with his other priorities such as the cost of living and re-industrialisation.
Others worry that the all-consuming nature of the EU debate means that it will drown out the other parts of the 10-year plan.
Watch: 'Hard Brexit we were given not good enough for Britain,' says Burnham
What remains unclear is the timeframe for the process that will follow Burnham setting out what he sees as the different Brexit options.
The prime minister has always been clear that Labour's commitments in its 2024 manifesto not to rejoin the single market or the customs union - let alone the EU altogether - still stand until the next general election.
And it was to those manifesto red lines that Burnham returned when asked about rejoining the EU at PMQs on Wednesday.
Yet those would not preclude Burnham initiating negotiations now on an arrangement breaking those red lines, which would take effect after the next general election.
Nevertheless, some on the prime minister's own side ponder that - having turned the volume up on the whole issue this autumn - he might be wise to turn it down a little in the new year, so it doesn't risk drowning out other things ministers want to talk about.
Andy Burnham is a prime minister who likes to explore things out loud. It's part of what he sees as a new way of doing politics, where he answers questions honestly and is prepared to discuss ideas while they are being formed, not just after they are a settled position.
It is a style that seeks to present a sense of a desired direction, even if some of the specifics end up being walked back from.
But even though it might be some time before the government has an official position on the future relationship, plenty of people are discussing what might happen next.
"It is all go again! My inbox is full of the same old stuff I thought I'd seen the back of years ago," one senior figure told us.
There are some nerves in the Labour Party about what might happen next. MPs who we have spoken to hold a range of views, which shows why this won't be plain-sailing.
Some are worried about re-opening the debate, calling it "toxic".
Others worry that the prime minister could disappoint pro-EU voters if he doesn't go far enough.
Others still wonder if the argument has changed enough that voters would decide differently in a new referendum.
"Both sides need fresh arguments, not the ones we all got tired of last time," said one.
"If this just looks like politicians wanting to rejoin because they never got over leaving then it's dead on arrival.
"If we can show that actually this is being led by businesses, by farmers, by different parts of society who need to rejoin because of the ways Brexit has harmed them, then it's a different matter," said another.
And what would the new EU the UK could rejoin look like?
Some Labour MPs ponder that the EU is changing – with the possibility of more right-wing leaders at the top table. They question whether they would want to be part of that.
EU-UK talks going down to the wire, says No 10
Burnham to set out options next month for long-term EU relationship
The EU that Burnham is eyeing up is very different to the one Britain left
UK lost more than it gained from Brexit, Burnham says ahead of EU summit
A long standing diplomat from an EU member state said that the possibility of political change within the EU,alongside the recent offer of associate membership to Canadaand at least the possibility of a potential future arrangement with Ukraine after any peace deal, could mean Brussels becomes more open to looser forms of membership that it has not been willing to consider before.
But then there is Scotland. If the government backs another EU vote, some Scottish MPs worry it adds to the argument for another vote on Scottish independence.
Despite the warnings, plenty of MPs are delighted that the Europe debate is back on the agenda.
One summed it up like this: "It doesn't really matter to me at this point where the PM is heading on this – it's all good for appealing to progressive voters. Just being seen to talk about this even without it necessarily being clear what we're going to do is a big change from before."
That seems to be a prevailing mood at the moment. Lots of Labour MPs are happy the EU debate is back. But not all of them.
Andy Burnham will on Friday sign a new deal with the EU which ministers believe will drive economic growth and cut red tape for British businesses. It will be heralded as a new moment for the relationship.
But how much further could the reset go?
The government hasn't decided yet - but plenty of others have their own views.
