title: Badenoch defends amputee marathon runners claim in benefits cut row
summary: Paralympian Richard Whitehead had accused the Conservative leader of "weaponising" his sporting success.
body:
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has defended her suggestion that because double amputees run marathons more disabled people should work instead of claiming benefits.
Badenoch had used the examplewhen setting out her party's plans to cut welfare spending by £36bn a year.
Her comments were criticised by Paralympian Richard Whitehead, who accused her of "weaponising" his sporting success, while Prime Minister Andy Burnham called the Tory leader's words "crass and insensitive".
But in an interview with the BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Badenoch stood by the remarks, insisting that "if people even with significant problems can work, then those who have ADHD and mild anxiety should go to work".
Asked if she accepted the comments were insensitive, Badenoch said: "No, no, no. I do not accept it. I will speak the truth, and I will say what I believe is common sense. I will speak the truth, and I will say what I believe is common sense.
"What I know is that if people can work, then we should encourage them to work."
Badenoch acknowledged she had used "extreme examples to illustrate things", but added: "If someone can do that, then yes, your condition of ADHD or anxiety is mild."
"I will say things as they are. People may disagree with things that I say, and that's fine, this is a free country, people are free to disagree, but they know where I'm coming from," she said.
"I start from first principles: If you can work, you should work, and the Conservative Party is going to help you get a job."
Government backs welfare shake-up to prevent 'lost generation'
What are the government's options for reducing welfare spending?
In a speech setting out the Conservative Party's welfare plans last week, Badenoch said: "The reality is that millions of people can and do contribute to our economy, to their families, to their communities even when they face serious challenges.
"Double amputees run marathons. People who are housebound do wonderful creative work from home. People with autism run some of the biggest tech companies in the world."
Responding to her speech, Whitehead - a double amputee marathon runner who has won four Paralympic medals -said he was "gobsmacked that somebody's sporting success would be weaponised in this way",external.
In a post on social media,external, he also said: "Disability should never be judged through isolated examples of individual achievement, but through an understanding of the barriers people and families face every day.
"The fact that some double-leg amputees can run marathons does not mean that disability support is unnecessary.
"Equally, the fact that some people with ADHD thrive despite limited support does not mean that others do not need meaningful assistance."
Richard Whitehead celebrates after winning the mens 200m in 2016
As part of their plans to cut welfare spending, the Conservatives have proposed stopping people from claiming disability benefits for "milder mental health issues and neurodiversity conditions such as anxiety, depression and ADHD", as well as "routine back and joint pain".
The party says its proposals to overhaul sickness and disability benefits would save £13.7bn a year.
It would also invest £1bn into health support, so people no longer eligible for cash benefits can access treatment to support their conditions instead.

title: PM urges social media companies to 'show some decency' and take down Brand video
summary: The comments came after YouTube owner Google refused a government request to remove a clip posted by the wife of the jailed comedian in which he claims he is innocent.
body:
Social media companies should "show some decency and take these videos down", the prime minister has said, following a government attempt to have a YouTube video featuring a message from the jailed comedian removed.
The site's owner Google refused a government request to remove the clip posted by Brand's wife in which he claims his innocence, Whitehall sources have told the BBC.
Brand was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison after being convicted of rape and three counts of sexual assault.
Speaking following a Coalition of the Willing meeting in Berlin, Andy Burnham said it was "time that we focus on the victims and think about them," rather than "hearing from a convicted criminal".
He said: "I would call on those social media companies to take these interviews down. Why are we having to hear from him. We shouldn't be and certainly [victims] shouldn't be hearing from him."
But when pressed by the reporter if he wanted to change the law to take action, he replied: "I wouldn't leap to that. I would first say to the social media companies show some responsibility here, think of the victims - that's the main thing.
"Show some decency and take these videos down."
Google told BBC News it was "aware of the new content and our teams are investigating".
It added: "Wesuspended Russell Brand's channelfrom the YouTube Partner Program in September 2023. The channel has not been able to monetise on YouTube since then."
On Sunday, Laura Brand shared a video on their Sunday Service channel on the website and read out a message from her husband in which he said: "I am not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for."
The Prison Service of England and Wales asked for the video to be removed, on the basis it was offensive to Brand's victims and had reached a substantial audience.
A Ministry of Justice (MoJ) spokesperson said while "removal ultimately depends on the platform's own terms", the department strongly believes "YouTube should remove this content".
Russell Brand prison message 'appalling' and being investigated, No 10 says
Minister criticises media for 'amplifying' Russell Brand's prison message
Met Police investigating more 'potential criminal allegations' about Brand
The BBC was initially told a minister had met Google to request the deactivation of Brand's account.
The MoJ later clarified the request had focused on the controversial video, and it is now understood a minister did not meet Google and the request was made via an established mechanism the prison service has with tech companies to request deletion of material.
The BBC has been told that Google declined the request, saying that its rules had not been broken, but housing minister Matthew Pennycook - who described the video as "abhorrent" - told BBC Breakfast that the government remained in "close dialogue" with the company.
Jess Phillips, the former minister for safeguarding and violence against women and girls, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme the government "doesn't have the power to enforce that this video is taken down".
"It relies on YouTube, in this instance... to do the right thing, which is a much, much broader argument about whether Ofcom codes that are in the Online Safety Act are there actually to protect women," she said.
An Ofcom spokesperson said in a statement that the current guidance was ultimately voluntary, and "any changes to the legislation to make it mandatory would be a matter for government and parliament".
Phillips, describing Brand as an "absolute narcissist", suggested it was "very likely"  the government would look at introducing a second online safety act to address gaps in the current regulatory framework.
"Before, we haven't had prisoners who had massive YouTube followings," she said. "This is an entirely new era."
However, the BBC understands there are no new plans to update or bring fresh legislation governing online platforms as a result of Brand's case.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said she would not immediately demand Google remove the video, if she was in power - although agreed it was concerning "if people in prison are able to use other conduits to send messages".
Badenoch told Today, YouTube was a private platform, and demanding content be taken down "without looking at exactly whether a law has been broken is not where I would start from".
"If we want to make legislation for that, then we can look at that. But I'm quite worried about government intervening," she added.
Connie Shaw of the Free Speech Union backed Badenoch's comments, saying that "if we want to protect everyone's free speech, we have to protect the free speech of even the most heinous people".
Speaking to the BBC's Politics Live,  she said that it would "set a very dangerous precedent if we said that Russell Brand's wife is not able to express the fact that he rejects the fact that he has been found guilty".
Brand's message has prompted an investigation into whether he had broken prison rules.
Downing Street previously called the message "clearly appalling", adding: "Prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims, and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances."
Justice Secretary Alex Norris said the case was being "urgently investigated, and I expect action to be taken if he is found to have broken the rules".
Prisoners' phone conversations are routinely recorded, but not necessarily listened to by prison authorities. If Brand is found to have breached the rules, possible repercussions could include a temporary phone ban or live monitoring of his calls.
In 2022 notorious inmate Charles Bronson reportedly had restrictions placed on his phone use after he sent Sky News an unauthorised audio message about his bid for parole.
In recent years, Brand has positioned himself as a Christian influencer and has a large following.
Mia Latter, a woman who has made allegations against Brand, saidshe found the message shared by Laura Brand "upsetting"and was appalled to hear "this Christian message alongside absolute lies".
Latter, 37, has alleged she was raped by the comedian when she was 16. She was not a complainant in his recent criminal trial and he denies her claims.
"I just felt for those women that stood trial and everything they went through," she told BBC.
The video and the Brands' YouTube account are still available on the site, and also still active is Brand's X account, where a message last appeared on 11 November.
"There was never a Russell Brand, according to @meta," it read, referring to Meta's decision todisable Brand's social media accountson Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp.
"Thank God for @elonmusk," the message added, referring to X's owner, before concluding: "Stay tuned."
The BBC has approached X for comment; Musk himself has criticised Brand's conviction for historical sex offences.
Children's minister Josh MacAlister told the Today programme the Meta decision provided a clear template for taking action.
"Meta's community standards prohibit accounts owned by or run on behalf of convicted sex offenders, and it's as simple as that," he said. "Google should take this down."

title: Cleverly to run as Tory London mayor candidate
summary: The former home and foreign secretary has been a London Assembly member and fire authority chair.
body:
Sir James was named as the Conservative Party candidate on Thursday
Former home secretary and foreign secretary Sir James Cleverly has been selected as the Conservative candidate for mayor of London.
The MP for Braintree in Essex was chosen in a poll of party members in London, winning 86% of the vote.
Sir James saw off a challenge from Westminster City councillor Festus Akinbusoye and Richmond Park parliamentary candidate Sara Gezdari.
He said London's "best days are ahead if we make a change at the forthcoming election". The next mayoral election will be in May 2028.
Labour incumbent Lord Khan, first elected in 2016, is yet to confirm whether he will seek a fourth term.
Sir James, a former head of the London Fire Authority, was widely expected to win the nomination after he stood down from the shadow cabinet in August.
He said he would not seek re-selection as the candidate in his Essex seat at the next general election.
At the announcement of the result, he said Lord Khan was "letting London down".
Sir James added: "People are leaving London, or not choosing to come here in the first place - businesses, job creators, families leaving London - and by the time of the election in 2028, Khan will have been mayor for 12 years, and those two things are related.
"The problems London faces are the symptoms. Khan is the cause. When I ask Londoners, 'Do you feel safe walking home at night?', the answer is no."
"It's shameful, it's a failure, and it's not just crime.
"We have had the worst period of housebuilding since the Second World War and only the highest-earning Londoners can afford the cheapest houses in London."
Bridget Phillipson, chair of the Labour Party, said: "James Cleverly has a record of failure and now wants to inflict his disastrous CV on London.
"He backed a no-deal Brexit and Liz Truss's disastrous mini-budget, voted for cuts to policing and youth services and opposed action to clean up London's air.
"Londoners should never forgive and never forget the damage the Conservatives did to our capital."
Sir James, an Army reservist, represented the Tories on the London Assembly before his election as MP for Braintree in 2015.
After rising through the backbenches, he unsuccessfully ran for Conservative Party leader in 2024, losing out to Kemi Badenoch.
The only other confirmed party choice for the mayoral race is Laila Cunningham from Reform UK, whose candidacy was announced in January.
She told BBC London: "It's the Conservatives that cut police, they cut the magistrates' numbers, crime went up, they politicised stop and search, and as a result knife crime has gone up massively."
Sarah Olney and Rob Blackie are both candidates for the Liberal Democrats' nomination.
Olney, the MP for Richmond Park, told BBC London the city "really needs a champion but the Tories are not going to be able to effectively hold Labour to account given their record in the capital".
She added: "James Cleverley simply is not a credible contender for mayor of London.
"In the past decade he has enthusiastically championed Brexit and he was a huge supporter of Liz Truss's mini budget and both of those things have done so much damage to London."
Should Lord Khan decide not to run again, there are a number of London Labour figures with ambitions to be the next mayor, including MPs Dawn Butler and Rosena Allin-Khan.
The Green Party, which won outright control of three London boroughs at the local elections in May, leads minority administrations in Haringey and Lambeth, and runs Southwark in coalition with the Lib Dems, has yet to begin the process of picking a candidate for the 2028 mayoral race.
Mayor of Hackney Zoë Garbett, who was the Green candidate in the 2024 mayoral election, said Sir James would "take London backwards".
She added: "Cleverly's platform is all about dividing our communities and making people's lives harder and more expensive."
